books.section: Bacon's Rebellion and the Development of Slavery in Virginia

options.misconception: The Navigation Acts regulated trade; they never banned indentured servants.
options.text: The Navigation Acts banned the use of indentured servants in Virginia.
Bacon's Rebellion showed planters that landless servants could unite across racial lines.

options.misconception: Tobacco still needed workers; high prices would mean more workers, not fewer.
options.text: Tobacco prices rose so high that planters no longer needed workers at all.

options.misconception: The king issued no order freeing indentured servants.
options.text: The king ordered all colonies to free their indentured servants at once.

rationales.A: The Navigation Acts regulated trade; they never banned indentured servants.
rationales.B: In Bacon's Rebellion, former indentured servants allied with free Black people along class lines, and that alliance frightened Virginia's planters. Background: Princeton notes the rebellion showed landowners it was not in their interest to have many landless, young, white men in the colony. Planters turned instead to enslaved African labor — workers bound for life and divided from servants by race. The Navigation Acts never banned servants, tobacco still needed workers, and the king issued no such order.
rationales.C: Tobacco still needed workers; high prices would mean more workers, not fewer.
rationales.D: The king issued no order freeing indentured servants.
rationales.general:
1. Read the 1676 row. Former servants and free Black people united against the Virginia government.
2. Ask what planters learned. A labor force that could unite across racial lines was dangerous to them.
3. Ask what they wanted instead. Workers bound for life and divided from servants by race.
4. Name the shift. After 1676 planters turned increasingly to enslaved African labor.
Remember: a rebellion teaches its losers and its winners — the planters learned to divide their workers.

source: original; stimulus is an original data table compiled from the grounding books
stem: Which development best explains why Virginia planters increasingly turned to enslaved labor after 1676?

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the grounding books; see grounding.
stimulus.text:
| Year | Development |
| 1619 | About twenty Africans arrive in Virginia; their status is not yet clearly defined |
| 1640 | John Punch, an African servant who ran away, is sentenced to serve for life |
| 1662 | Virginia's partus sequitur ventrum law: a child's status follows the mother's, making slavery hereditary |
| 1676 | Bacon's Rebellion: former servants and free Black people unite against the Virginia government |
| 1705 | Virginia's slave code defines enslaved people as property for life |
